scenes.name: Rapcore y New Metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Body Count, el grupo del rapero Ice-T, abre el rapcore con temas atractivos para chicos de todas las razas; a finales de la década las voces rapeadas se ponen de moda, aunque pocos de esos grupos son metal. Spin dedica en agosto de 1998 un reportaje al «New Metal» (Korn, Limp Bizkit con su DJ fijo), un híbrido que bebe tanto del rock alternativo, el hip-hop y el hardcore del skate californiano como de Black Sabbath y Slayer, y Rolling Stone lleva en febrero de 1999 a Rob Zombie en portada con los «10 mejores grupos de metal». Weinstein se pregunta por qué se llama metal a lo que sus músicos no quieren que se llame así: la etiqueta da una imagen más blanca y más rock, y su uso promiscuo es a la vez prueba y causa del regreso del metal. ¿Es metal Rage Against the Machine? ¿Y Sevendust o Limp Bizkit?

podcast.title: Encounter with Fred Durst (Early 1995)
podcast.body: In early 1995, while Korn was on tour promoting their recently released debut album, they encountered Fred Durst in Jacksonville, Florida. Durst, a tattoo artist and an ardent fan, offered the band members free tattoos. "In early 1995, Corn was on a tour that brought them through town."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: The Crow: City of Angels Soundtrack Contribution (1996)
podcast.body: Korn was featured on the soundtrack for *The Crow: City of Angels*, the 1996 sequel to *The Crow*. This collection was considered "pretty much as good as the first one" and included other prominent bands of the era. "Bush, Corn, Deftones, E-Pop, White Zombie, Filter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Project Revolution Performer (2004)
podcast.body: Korn performed at Project Revolution in 2004, which expanded into a two-stage event featuring ten performers. "featuring 10 performers including their buddies in Corn"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 2006 Blood Disorder and Tour Cancellation
podcast.body: In the spring of 2006, at the peak of Korn's success, Jonathan Davis began experiencing strange bruises and extreme weakness after gigs. He was diagnosed with Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), a blood infection caused by an allergic reaction to medication, which drastically lowered his blood platelet count to five (normal range is 140-400). While on tour in the UK, all further shows were canceled due to the risk of a brain hemorrhage from his constant head banging. "It turns out he had something called immune frombocytopetic perpera. This is a type of blood infection brought on, in Jonathan's case, by an allergic reaction to some medication he'd been taking. IMP results in low blood platelet count, meaning that Jonathan's blood had difficulty clotting. That explains the bruises. A normal count is between 140 and 400. Jonathan's count was five. Had he continued, Jonathan would have been in danger of having a brain hemorrhage because he was head banging all the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Active Rock Radio Benefit (2010s)
podcast.body: This band, identified as one of the most successful survivors of the nu metal era, benefited from promotion on active rock radio stations in the 2010s. "This included corn and slipknot, the two most successful survivors of the new metal era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Apollo Theater Performance
podcast.body: Korn made history by becoming the first rock band to perform at the legendary Apollo Theater in Harlem, a significant achievement that demonstrated their mainstream acceptance and crossover appeal. "Corn also became the first rock band to play the Apollo Theater in Harlem, and if that doesn't demonstrate a certain level of mainstream acceptance, I don't know what will."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Childhood Asthma
podcast.body: As a child, Jonathan Davis suffered from a severe case of asthma that led to multiple hospitalizations and nearly caused his death on several occasions. "When he was a kid, he had a really, really bad case of asthma, so bad that he ended up in the hospital a bunch of times. In fact, he nearly died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Contemporary Catalog Sale
podcast.body: Korn is included in a list of modern acts that have sold some or all of their back catalog, signifying the widespread adoption of this financial strategy across different genres and artist demographics.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 2

podcast.title: Controversial Album Art
podcast.body: The cover art for Korn's debut album was considered so creepy and sinister that Justine Ferrarra, the eight-year-old model, was not shown the final picture until she reached the eighth grade. Furthermore, the family of Paul Pontius, her uncle and an Immortal Records employee, expressed significant displeasure with the unsettling results of the album's artwork. "Little Justine wasn't shown the picture until she was in the eighth grade, simply because it's so creepy and sinister."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Dreadlocks in 1990s Rock and Metal
podcast.body: Jonathan Davis of KoRn notably wore dreadlocks throughout the 1990s, contributing to the hairstyle's popularization among musicians in the rock and metal genres. "And then through the 90s, dreads appeared on everyone from Rob Zombie and Zach from Raging Us the Machine to Jonathan Davis of Corn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Good Rhythm Section
podcast.body: Korn is briefly mentioned as a band possessing a "pretty good" rhythm section, highlighting their contribution to the overall sound. "A corn is pretty good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Head Receives Korn Tattoo from Fred Durst
podcast.body: During a tour stop in Jacksonville, Florida, in early 1995, Korn guitarist Head was the only band member to accept Fred Durst's offer of a free tattoo. Head received a "substantive looking Korn logo" tattooed on his back. This seemingly minor interaction proved pivotal for Durst's future career. "No one took them up on it except head, one of the guitars who got a pretty substantive looking Corn logo on his back."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: Influence from Body Count
podcast.body: KoRn is part of the lineage of bands influenced by Body Count, connecting them to the origins of the nu-metal movement. "So basically, you can draw a line from Body Count, right through corn, slipknot, and limp biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspired by Skinny Puppy
podcast.body: Korn is explicitly listed as an artist who was inspired and influenced by the Canadian industrial band Skinny Puppy. "Here's a short list of artists who say they were inspired and influenced by Skinny Puppy, Ministry, Nine-inch Nails, Maryland Manson, the Prodigy, Ramstein, Filter, Corn, Lincoln Park, Evan Essence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Introspective and Vulnerable Side
podcast.body: While intense, Korn's music also revealed an introspective, sensitive, and vulnerable side, distinguishing them from some of the more "fratboyish" aspects associated with new metal. "They were still very intense, but they also could have an introspective, sensitive, and vulnerable side."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Jonathan Davis's Background
podcast.body: Lead singer Jonathan Davis previously worked as an "apprentice mortician," with one of his old jobs involving picking up bodies at traffic accident scenes. "Led by an apprentice mortician named Jonathan Davis, one of his old jobs was to pick up bodies at traffic accidents scenes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jonathan Davis's Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura from Headbanging
podcast.body: In 2006, Jonathan Davis noticed purple blotches and bruising on his legs, which led to a diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenic purpura, a blood clotting disorder. Doctors advised him that had he continued headbanging on stage, he could have suffered a brain hemorrhage and died. "And according to doctors, had he continued to head bang on stage, he could have had a brain hemorrhage and died right there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Korn T-Shirt Banned at Michigan School – Legal Threat Issued
podcast.body: A Michigan secondary school (Zeeland) banned clothing bearing the Korn name or imagery, describing the band as "indecent, vulgar, and obscene," while simultaneously allowing Limp Bizkit merchandise. Korn threatened a lawsuit in response. "The school banned Korn clothing, describing the band as 'indecent, vulgar, and obscene,' while allowing Limp Bizkit, leading Korn to threaten a lawsuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lyrical Themes
podcast.body: Lyrically, the band focused on themes of "personal tragedy and angst and fear," and they were known for "turn[ing] everything up to 11." "Now, lyrically, the band was focused on personal tragedy and angst and fear. And then they turned everything up to 11."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Managed by The Firm
podcast.body: Korn was managed by The Firm, a powerful agency that also handled the careers of Linkin Park, Ice Cube, and American Idol winner Taylor Hicks. "the manager was a powerful agency called The Firm, which also runs the careers of everyone from corn to ice cube to American Idol Taylor Hicks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Model on Debut Album Cover
podcast.body: The young girl featured on Korn's 1994 self-titled debut album cover is Justine Ferrarra, who was eight years old at the time. She is the niece of Paul Pontius, an employee at Korn's then-label, Immortal Records, and was paid $300 for her participation in the photoshoot. "The little girl's name is Justine Ferrarra."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Most Successful New Metal Band
podcast.body: Korn is considered "probably" the most successful of all the new metal bands. "The most successful of all the new metal bands is probably corn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Influences and Sound
podcast.body: Korn took what Rage Against the Machine was doing, incorporated a "healthy dose of grunge," and then mixed in elements of Cypress Hill, creating a distinctive sound. "Corn took what rage against the machine was doing, added in a healthy dose of grunge and then mixed in a bunch of Cypress Hill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins in California Desert
podcast.body: The band emerged from the California desert in the early 1990s. "who came out of the California desert in the early 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Partial Catalog Sale
podcast.body: Korn is mentioned as an artist who has sold only a portion of their song catalog, rather than the entire portfolio. "It's like corn, tom de long, Dave Navarro and many others have sold just a portion of their portfolio of songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pivotal Tattoo Offer for Limp Bizkit's Success
podcast.body: The decision by Korn's guitarist Head to accept a free tattoo from Fred Durst was a pivotal moment. This interaction led Durst to send Limp Bizkit's demo to Korn members, which ultimately secured Limp Bizkit's major label deal and their rise in the nu-metal scene. Without Head's acceptance and Durst's belief in his own band, Limp Bizkit's career might not have materialized as it did. "None of this would have happened had head from Corn not taken up Fred on his offer for free tattoo and had Fred not had a little faith in his new band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: Recovery from ITP
podcast.body: Jonathan Davis spent four days in the hospital for his Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) and underwent a three-week regimen of steroids to restore his blood platelet count. He must still be cautious about his condition. "He was in the hospital for four days, and it took about three weeks for his blood to get back in order with a regiment of steroids. He still has to be careful."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tattoo Admiration by Darren Fyfer
podcast.body: The members of KoRn, specifically Fieldy and Jonathan (presumably Jonathan Davis), are admired by Goldfinger drummer Darren Fyfer for their "super into" and "really nice tattoos." "All the guys in court. All those guys are super into like fieldy and Jonathan. They got some really nice tattoos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tour Exhaustion
podcast.body: Lead singer Jonathan Davis describes the extreme physical and mental drain of performing longer sets (an hour to an hour and twenty minutes) on tour, contrasting it with the relative ease of earlier 45-minute sets. He notes that by the end of such shows, he is completely drained, often feeling "done" after just three songs into a headlining set. "Usually by the end of the show, mostly the drylands gone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Woodstock 99 Performance and Crowd Demeanor
podcast.body: Korn was part of the lineup at Woodstock 99, which featured a concentration of "intense and angry new metal bands." This lineup contributed to an atmosphere of heightened "male rage and testosterone" among the 200,000 attendees, a key factor in the eventual escalation to widespread violence and property damage. "Added in the fact that the lineup was filled with intense and angry new metal bands, LeBiscuit corn, kid rocked, rage guns, the machine, Metallica, tons of mail rage and testosterone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Youth Identity Expression - 1990s
podcast.body: In the 1990s, young people expressed their identity and tastes by wearing t-shirts of artists like Korn. This was part of a broader cultural trend where urban tribes lived their golden age. "vistiendo camisetas de Marilyn Manson o Corn."
